full_judgment:
21. Now let us examine as to whether it was at all possible for the P.Ws.1 to 6 to see as to who actually fired the two gun shots on Golam Mustafa. P.W. I stated in her evidence that "there is completely open space between our house and the railway track". This evidence of P.W. 1 is not consistent with the prosecution case. All the witnesses consistently stated that the Rajakars asked Galim Mustafa to cut down jungles around the house, which means that there were jungles on all sides of the house, P.W. 1 has been clearly contradicted by P.Ws. 3 and 6. P.W. 3 stated in cross-examination that "The jungles were on the western side of the house of Dula Mia". P.W. 6 stated in cross-examination "The jungles were on the west and north of our house". Thus it appears that P.W. 1 did not tell the truth when she stated that "There is completely open space between our house and the railway track." And it is further clear that P.W. 1 made the said statement because she must have felt that open space would be necessary to make her recognition of the killer credible to the court. Therefore there being jungles on the western and northern side of the house of Dula Mia, it is improbable that the witnesses could see the actual occurrence, namely, alleged firing of rifle shots at the deceased by the appellant and thereby killing him then and there on the railway track. Even if we accept that the witnesses saw the two Rajakars dragging Golam Mustafa to the nearby railway track beating with rifle butts, and heard two rifle shots, it is difficult to accept the prosecution case that the witnesses saw the appellant killing Golam Mustafa by firing two rifle shots. This part of their evidence is based on presumption that one of the two Rajakars must have fired his rifle and the same must have killed Golam Mustafa. We have been from the evidence that P.Ws. 1 to 6 stated that Golam Mustafa fell down on the ground after two rifle shots, and immediately thereafter there were several blank shots in the air when continuous firing started from the local Pakistan Military Camp at a distance of the mile which made all the witnesses and other inmates of the neighbouring houses panicky and all of them hurriedly let the village. Admittedly the witnesses saw the incident from a considerable distance, we accept that all of them were actually present, but none of the witnesses, not even P.W. 1 dared to go to the place where the injured Golam Mustafa fell down That is to say, none of the witnesses actually saw the injuries caused if any by the two rifle shots or saw Golam Mustafa dead. Their evidence or this point is purely based on presumption and guess, and it does not provide any direct evidence, that Golam Mustafa received two bullet injuries and on account of those injuries died on the spot. It is indirect evidence and being presumptive in character is very weak piece of evidence. Such evidence cannot be made the basis of conviction under section 302 of the Penal Code. Therefore we find that there is a gap in the prosecution evidence to connect the two Rajakars with the death of Golam Mustafa on account of two rifle shots. It is not improbable that Golam Mustafa being tired, as he was fasting, could not stand the beating with rifle butts and as a result he fell down unconscious or he might have fallen down on receiving the bullet shots on any part of the body or he might have fallen down out of fright when rifle shots were being fired. Therefore possibility of Golam Mustafa falling down unconscious either on receiving the rifle shots or hearing the sounds of the two rifle shots or falling down out of exhaustion, cannot altogether be ruled out. Even if we forget about the existence of jungles on the western and the northern side of the house, this part of the evidence of the witnesses, cannot be accepted as the direct evidence, because, whatever they said, they said on the basis of mere inference and guess. When a person sees another person at a considerable distance being fired at by a gun and he falls down on the ground, the person seeing the occurrence may presume that the man was killed by gun shots. Until he goes to the spot and observes the injured man, he cannot definitely say as to whether the man was injured or dead or alive. That is exactly the position in this case. Another possibility in this case cannot be ruled out, namely, Golam Mustafa might have fallen down unconscious either on receiving the bullet injury on even without any bullet injury, and while he was continuing in the state of unconsciousness dogs and jackals fell upon him and devoured him. This was not impossible, because, the incident took place shortly before sunset and there were jungles around, and there was none to give any protection to Golam Mustafa lying on the ground. Therefore this raises a reasonable doubt in our mind as to whether Golam Mustafa was killed by the two Rajakars by two rifle shots as alleged by the prosecution. 

 26. Presence of the corpus delicti is no doubt proof positive of the death but its absence is not fatal to the trial of the accused for murder. Literal meaning of the term corpus delicti is "body of the offence", that is, the ingredients which go to make it up. The expression corpus delicti has been used in the penal laws of this sub-continent rather loosely to signify the body of the murdered man in cases of murder. However, in view of the definition of "proved" in the Evidence Act, there is no room for the "body" doctrine. Absence of the body is not fatal to the trial of a murder case, provided there is sufficient evidence to conclusively prove the death as alleged by the prosecution. In the instant case the "body" doctrine has relevancy. None of the witnesses saw Golam Mustafa actually dead or that Golam Mustafa received the bullet injuries as alleged by the prosecution. The entire evidence on this point is based on presumption and inference from the circumstances. There is no direct evidence to prove the prosecution case. In spite of our serious consideration of the entire evidence we are constrained to hold that the prosecution failed to prove the manner of the occurrence as alleged by the prosecution.
